Finite Potential Well — Bound States
✦Ask Euler i

About the simulation

Physics. This uses the lecture convention for the finite well: V(x) = -V0 for |x| < a and V(x) = 0 outside, so the well has width 2a. Bound states have negative energy, oscillate inside the well, and decay exponentially in the classically forbidden region |x| > a.

Display. The upper panel shows the potential and the selected bound-state energy. The lower panel shows the actual wavefunction and probability density with their own labeled vertical scales, so no hidden peak-rescaling is used.

Assumptions. Numerical values are shown using a fixed particle mass equal to one electron mass. Keeping the mass fixed narrows the model compared with the symbolic lecture notes, but makes the plotted energies and decay lengths concrete.

Controls. V0 changes the well depth and 2a changes the well width. Animation speed only changes the phase rotation of Ψ. Choose n with ◀ ▶, the energy list, or ↑/↓. Reset restores defaults; Pause or space stops time.

Guided Inquiry

1 · A well with a rim

Here’s our well. A particle sits in a well of depth V₀ and width 2a — finitely deep, unlike the impenetrable box. The upper panel plots the potential and the energy of the selected bound state. The lower panel plots the wave Ψ(x,t) and the probability density |ψ(x)|², with the region beyond the walls shaded.

2 · A classical marble

Let’s start with something familiar. Take a classical marble in this well, with energy below the rim. Over many observations, where do you think it’s found?

3 · Past the wall

Now the quantum version. The ground state n = 1 is drawn, and its wave doesn’t stop at the wall: beyond it the curve falls away smoothly instead of oscillating. What do you think accounts for that shape?

4 · Which state reaches furthest

Time to explore. Hold V₀ and 2a fixed and step through the four bound states. Which one do you think keeps the largest share of its probability beyond the walls?

5 · How many rungs fit

Now let’s squeeze the well. Make it shallower and narrower: V₀ down to 5, 2a down to 0.20. What do you think becomes of the list of bound states?

6 · The price of a soft wall

One last question. At n = 1 the wave continues past the wall instead of being cut off there. How does that compare with an impenetrable box of the same width 2a? This well’s ground-state energy is…

The Physics

Finite potential well · what this sim shows, the physics behind it, and every control

01

At a glance

This sim shows what the wave of a quantum particle does at the walls of a finite potential well, and how many bound states the well holds. Real walls have finite height, and this is the simplest model that includes that.

What you'll learn

  • How the wave behaves at the walls and beyond them.
  • How the state number n sets the energy and the probability found outside the well.
  • How the depth V₀ and the width 2a set the number of bound states.
  • How the Ψ curves and the |ψ|² curve differ for a state of definite energy.
The model: depth V₀, width 2a. The sim measures energy from the rim, where V = 0.

What's on screen

  • Blue line (upper panel): the potential V(x), with dashed walls at x = ±a.
  • Yellow dashed line: the selected state's energy, labelled n and E.
  • Coloured curve (lower panel): Re Ψ, pink for n = 1. The purple curve is Im Ψ.
  • Green curve and fill: the probability density |ψ|², on its own scale. |x| > a is shaded.
  • Sidebar: Energy, Probability outside well, and the list of bound states.
See itOpen the default well on its lowest state, n = 1. Watch for: the blue well in the upper panel with the yellow dashed energy line inside it, and the pink Ψ curve with the green |ψ|² fill below.

03

Oscillating inside, decaying outside

The potential is V = −V₀ for |x| < a and V = 0 for |x| > a. A bound state has an energy between the floor and the rim:

The well, and the energy window a bound state must sit in.

The time-independent Schrödinger equation then has a different form on each side of the wall, set by the sign of E − V:

Inside, E > V. Outside, E < V.
  • Inside, ψ is a sine or cosine with wavenumber k.
  • Outside, the solution that grows with |x| cannot be normalised, so only the decaying exponential remains. It never reaches zero.
  • At the wall, V jumps by a finite amount, so ψ and ψ′ are continuous there. The wave does not stop at x = ±a. E is the same on both sides; only the sign of E − V changes.
See itLook at the default well on n = 1, where the dashed lines mark the walls. Watch for: the pink curve and the green fill continuing past the dashed walls, bending smoothly into the shaded region instead of stopping.
04

How far the tail reaches

Outside the walls, ψ falls as e−κ(|x|−a), with κ = √(2m|E|)/ħ. The rim is at E = 0, so |E| is how far the level lies below it. The decay length 1/κ is the distance over which ψ falls by a factor e.

The share outside is the area under |ψ|² beyond the walls, as a fraction of the total area, which is 1.
  • At the default well (V₀ = 20 eV, 2a = 0.50 nm), n = 1 has E = −18.913 eV, 1/κ = 0.045 nm and 0.83% outside. n = 4 has E = −3.763 eV, 1/κ = 0.101 nm and 23.30% outside.
  • Closer to the rim means smaller κ, a longer tail and a larger share outside. As |E| goes to zero, 1/κ grows without limit.
The tail past the wall at the default well, for n = 1 and n = 4. Dotted lines mark 1/κ.
See itTake the default well on n = 1, then on n = 4. Watch for: the Outside well readout going from 0.83% to 23.30% as the green fill and the Ψ curves beyond the dashed walls grow.
05

The number of levels depends on one number

Matching ψ and ψ′ at x = a gives one condition for even states and one for odd states. Here z = ka and z₀ = a√(V₀/(ħ²/2m)):

The two quantisation conditions.
Each crossing of a branch with the circle κa = √(z₀² − z²) is one bound state. Here z₀ = 5.73, so there are four.
The energies, and the number of levels.
V₀ 2a

These sliders move the sim too.

  • Counting. V₀ and a enter the count only through z₀. A new level appears each time z₀ passes a multiple of π/2, alternately even and odd. A one-dimensional well always holds at least one. At the default well, a = 0.25 nm and z₀ = 0.25·√(20/0.0381) = 5.73, so N = ⌈3.65⌉ = 4.
  • Scaling. Double 2a and divide V₀ by 4: z₀, N and every zn stay the same, so every En becomes exactly one quarter. For n = 1, −18.913 eV becomes −4.728 eV.
See itMake the well as shallow and narrow as the sliders allow: V₀ = 5 eV, 2a = 0.20 nm. Watch for: the list of bound states shrinking to a single entry, n = 1 at about −2.57.
See itTake the default well, then V₀ = 5 eV with 2a = 1.00 nm. Watch for: the n = 1 Energy going from −18.913 to −4.728, a quarter of the first value, with four levels in the list both times.
06

A soft wall lowers every level

An infinitely deep box of the same width 2a has its ground state at E = ħ²π²/(2m(2a)²). For 2a = 0.50 nm that is 1.504 eV above the floor. The sim does not draw a box; this number is calculated here.

  • The finite well is lower. Its ground state, −18.913 eV, lies 1.087 eV above the floor at −20 eV.
  • Why. The wave continues past the walls, so inside the well it turns through less than the box's half wavelength: ka = z₁ < π/2, where the box has exactly π/2. A smaller k means less kinetic energy.
  • Every level. zn lies between (n−1)π/2 and nπ/2, so each level lies below the box level of the same n. A deeper well approaches the box: at V₀ = 50 eV the ground state is 1.219 eV above the floor.
See itLook at the ground state of the default well. Watch for: the yellow dashed line just above the well's floor, with Energy reading −18.913, which is 1.087 above −20.
07

A stationary state keeps its density

A state of definite energy has one phase factor in time, and it cancels in the density:

Ψ(x,t) = ψ(x) e−iEt/ħ.
  • Two curves turn. The coloured curve is Re Ψ and the purple curve is Im Ψ. They trade height as the phase advances.
  • One curve stays. The green |ψ|² never moves. This is what "stationary" means.
  • Animation speed is a display rate. The sim turns the phase at a rate set by max(|E|, 0.25) times the speed slider, not at the true |E|/ħ, which is about 2.9×10¹⁶ rad/s for n = 1 at the default well, with E measured from the rim. The sense of rotation on screen is also a display choice.
See itRun n = 4 at speed 1× with both curve toggles on. Watch for: the coloured and purple curves trading height while the green |ψ|² fill stays put.
08

Where it matters

  • Semiconductor quantum wells. A thin GaAs layer between AlGaAs layers is a well for electrons, a few nm wide and a few tenths of an eV deep, and quantum-well lasers use it. The electron's effective mass there is about 0.067 mₑ, so this sim's numbers do not carry over, but the physics does.
  • Scanning tunnelling microscopy. The same decay law makes the tunnelling current between tip and surface fall as e−2κd with the gap d. For a work function of 4 to 5 eV, κ is about 10 to 11 nm⁻¹, so each extra 0.1 nm of gap cuts the current by about 8 to 10 times.
Go deeper: two more cases
  • The deuteron. Its s-wave radial problem is the odd sector of this well. With V₀ = 35 MeV and a = 2 fm, the binding comes out near 1.7 MeV, against 2.22 MeV measured, with about two-thirds of the probability outside the force range.
  • Two energies at once. Take (ψ₁ + ψ₄)/√2 at the default well. The density then oscillates at (E₄ − E₁)/ħ, with a period near 0.27 fs. The sim shows single states only.
09

Summary

In one line. A bound state oscillates inside the well and decays outside it, so some probability lies beyond the walls, more for levels closer to the rim.

Key points

  • Bound energies lie between −V₀ and 0. The tail decays over 1/κ = ħ/√(2m|E|).
  • The number of levels is N = ⌈2z₀/π⌉, never less than 1.
  • Every level lies below the infinite-box level of the same n and width.

Common mix-ups

  • "With energy below the rim, the particle stays between the walls." A classical marble would. The quantum state has probability beyond the walls, and the sim prints it.
  • "The most tightly bound state reaches furthest." The reverse: κ grows with |E|, so n = 1 has the shortest tail.

Things to try on your own

  • At the default well, step through n = 1 to 4 and note Probability outside well for each, beside its distance below the rim.
  • Keep 2a = 0.50 nm and lower V₀ until the list drops from four levels to three. Compare with 13.54 eV, where z₀ = 3π/2.
  • Set V₀ = 50 eV, 2a = 0.50 nm. From Energy, find how far the ground state sits above the floor, and compare with the box value, 1.504 eV.
